# RihVerb

**Algorithmic Reverb with Swell and Tonal Drift**

A VST3 reverb for Windows. An eight line feedback delay network fed alongside a tapped
early reflection cluster, with two controls that ordinary reverbs do not have: Bloom
pours the signal into the tank over time so the tail swells in, and Gravity sweeps the
tone of the tail as it decays. Written in C++17 on JUCE.

![RihVerb main window](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ClyntiaAikaHanaa/RihVerb/HEAD/Screenshot/Main.png)

## What it does

Most algorithmic reverbs give you the same six controls, and they all shape a tail that
behaves the same way: it starts loud the instant the source arrives, and it gets quieter
and duller from there. Anything else means bouncing audio out, reversing it, and flying it
back in, or drawing filter automation across every tail by hand.

RihVerb keeps those six controls and adds two that change the shape of the tail itself.

**Bloom** spreads the late reverb send backwards in time. Instead of the source hitting the
tank all at once, a bank of taps pours it in gradually with a rising weight, so the tail
builds up rather than starting at full level. The reverb gets longer by the swell time, not
shorter, which is the difference between a swell and a gate. It is deterministic, so it
behaves the same on a sustained pad as it does on a drum hit.

**Gravity** moves the tone of the tail across its own lifetime. At zero the tail keeps a
constant colour. Turn it down and the tail closes in on itself, getting darker the longer it
rings. Turn it up and it opens outward instead, a character that is hard to get any other
way. This is separate from Dampen, which sets a fixed amount of absorption, so the two do
not fight each other.

Three things shape the design:

1. **The tail is the instrument.** Bloom and Gravity both act on how the tail evolves over
   time, not on a static setting applied to it.
2. **Zero reported latency.** No lookahead and no FFT, so it stays usable while tracking.
3. **You can see what you hear.** The halo around the sphere is the actual wet envelope of
   the last four seconds, so a long Decay stretches it and Bloom visibly swells it.

## Features

### Engine

* Eight line feedback delay network with Hadamard mixing, using a Walsh Hadamard butterfly
  so the whole matrix costs 24 additions per sample rather than 64 multiply accumulates.
* Mutually prime line lengths with a slow per line modulation, which keeps the modal
  density smooth and prevents the metallic ringing a fixed network produces.
* Separate early reflection stage: eight taps per channel into three Schroeder allpass
  diffusers, with tap times scaled by Size.
* Feedback gains solved from the target decay time, so Decay reads as an actual RT60 rather
  than an arbitrary feedback number.
* Delay lengths are derived in seconds and converted at the current rate, so the character
  holds from 44.1 kHz to 192 kHz.

### Signature controls

* **Bloom** builds the swell from 20 jittered taps with a rising weight profile, energy
  normalised, followed by two allpass diffusers and an 80 Hz high pass so each tap becomes a
  cloud instead of an audible echo and the low end does not pile up in the tank. Swell time
  scales with Decay, up to 2.5 seconds.
* **Gravity** sweeps the in loop damping corner across five octaves over the age of the
  tail, plus a two stage output tilt of 10 dB per stage at 400 Hz and 2.5 kHz. The tail
  clock is restarted by a ratio based transient detector, so a new hit starts a new sweep.
* Both are smoothed at control rate, which keeps the filter coefficients free of zipper
  noise even at short decay settings.

### Controls

| Control | Range | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decay | 0.1 s to 20 s | Length of the tail, as an RT60 |
| Dampen | 0 to 100 percent | Fixed high frequency absorption in the feedback loop |
| Size | 0 to 100 percent | Scale of the simulated space, from a tight room to a hall |
| Predelay | 0 to 250 ms | Holds the whole wet path back behind the dry signal |
| Early | 0 to 100 percent | Balance between early reflections and the diffuse tail |
| Width | 0 to 100 percent | Stereo spread of the reverb, mono through to full width |
| Mix | 0 to 100 percent | Dry and wet balance |
| Bloom | 0 to 100 percent | Swell time, from an immediate tail to a full fade in |
| Gravity | -100 to +100 percent | Tonal drift across the tail, darker or brighter |

### Interface

* Animated sphere driven by the plugin state: radius follows Size, orbit speed follows
  Decay, mesh density follows Dampen, and the surrounding halo is the real wet envelope.
* Every motion runs off an accumulator wrapped at two pi and advanced by elapsed time, so
  the animation never jumps at a wrap and an uneven timer cannot make it stutter.
* Resizable from 72 percent to 250 percent by dragging the bottom right corner. The whole
  interface lives in one fixed coordinate space and is scaled by a single transform, so
  every stroke width, gap and font tracks the render scale exactly.
* Double click any knob to type an exact value.
* Dice button in the title bar rolls a new value for every control, wrapped in a single
  host gesture so it is one undo step.
* Status bar describes whichever control is under the pointer.

## Project layout

```
Source/
  ReverbEngine.h    engine: FDN, early reflections, predelay, Bloom, Gravity
  PluginProcessor.* parameters, buses, state
  PluginEditor.*    fixed size canvas, scaled by a single transform
  UI/
    Theme.h         palette, fonts and the base design size
    Widgets.*       knobs with inline value entry, meter, header, dice
    Visualizer.*    sphere, orbits and the wet envelope halo
Tools/
  logoexport.cpp    brand asset and screenshot exporter
Branding/           generated mark and badge PNGs
Screenshot/
  Logo.png          README logo, built by make_logo.ps1
  Main.png          README screenshot, rendered by the exporter
```

Version 1 ships a single init state and no preset browser. Parameter values and the editor
size are saved with the host project.
